*Updated October 2026.*

"Should we use RAG or fine-tuning?" is one of the most common — and most misunderstood — questions in enterprise AI. Vendors push fine-tuning because it sounds sophisticated. Most businesses need RAG. Here is how to tell which one you actually need.

## The one-paragraph version

**RAG** connects the model to your documents at query time — the model looks up relevant passages, then answers from them. **Fine-tuning** retrains the model on your data, baking knowledge into its weights. RAG is cheaper, faster to update, and every answer can cite its source. Fine-tuning is better for teaching style, tone, and behavior — not facts.

## When RAG wins

- **Your knowledge changes.** Prices, policies, product docs, tickets — RAG updates by re-indexing a document. Fine-tuning requires retraining.
- **You need citations.** RAG answers point back to source documents. Fine-tuned models cannot tell you where an answer came from.
- **Accuracy matters more than style.** RAG grounds answers in retrieved text; fine-tuned models still hallucinate, just more confidently.
- **You have a budget.** RAG pilots start around $12,000–$18,000. Fine-tuning pipelines with proper evaluation start higher and cost more to maintain.

## When fine-tuning wins

- **You need a specific voice or format.** Customer-facing copy in your brand voice, structured outputs in an exact schema, domain-specific reasoning patterns.
- **The task is behavioral, not factual.** Teaching the model *how* to respond (tone, structure, refusal behavior) rather than *what* to know.
- **Latency is critical.** A fine-tuned smaller model can outperform a large model + retrieval pipeline on speed for narrow tasks.

## The option most people miss: both

The strongest production systems combine them. Fine-tune for behavior and format; use RAG for knowledge. A customer support AI might be fine-tuned on your tone guidelines while retrieving answers from your help center. This is more engineering work, but it is also the architecture behind the systems that actually survive contact with real users.

## The decision framework

Ask these three questions in order:

1. **Does the knowledge change?** Yes → RAG. Your docs update weekly; retraining monthly is absurd.
2. **Do answers need sources?** Yes → RAG. Compliance, legal, and support teams need audit trails.
3. **Is the problem style or facts?** Style → fine-tuning. Facts → RAG.

If you answered RAG to all three, you have your answer — and you are in the majority. Roughly 80% of enterprise "we need AI on our data" requests are RAG problems wearing fine-tuning clothes.

## Common traps

- **"Fine-tuning will stop hallucinations."** It won't. Fine-tuned models hallucinate with your vocabulary. Grounding (RAG) is what reduces fabrication.
- **"RAG is just a demo trick."** Naive RAG is. Production RAG — hybrid retrieval, permission-aware access, evaluation harnesses — is real engineering.
- **"We'll fine-tune on all our docs."** Training on documents teaches the model to *mimic* documents, not to *retrieve* facts from them. This is the most expensive way to learn this lesson.

## Cost comparison

| | RAG | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|
| Pilot build | $12,000–$18,000 | $20,000–$35,000 |
| Knowledge updates | Re-index (minutes) | Retrain (days, $1k+ each) |
| Citations | Yes, built in | No |
| Hallucination control | Groundedness checks | Limited |

See our full [RAG cost breakdown](/blog/how-much-does-rag-development-cost) for detailed numbers.

## The bottom line

Start with RAG. Add fine-tuning only when you have a specific behavioral problem that retrieval cannot solve. Your future self — the one not retraining a model every time a policy changes — will thank you.

If you want help deciding for your specific use case, [book a free consultation](/services/rag-development).
